role: Trusts and estates, with Warrick (wealth architecture)
title: Protect the base: four events, four protections
summary: Before you take developer-sized risks, protect against the four events that can undo everything regardless of how good your deals are: dying, losing the ability to decide, suffering a large loss, and losing income. This lesson maps each event to its protection: a will, powers of attorney, insurance and an emergency reserve. All as concepts; a licensed professional is required before you act.
body:
Your deals can be excellent and still fail you, because the person running them can die, fall ill, be sued or lose income. A will, powers of attorney, insurance and a reserve are the four protections that let your wealth survive you having a bad day.

Recall

Q. What four questions should you put to any personal guarantee?

A. How much is it capped at, what triggers it, when does it end, and must the lender pursue the company and the property before coming to you?

Q. What belongs in the first paragraph of a one-page memo?

A. The conclusion and the decision you need, so a reader who stops there can still act.

Q. Why does a developer need go/no-go gates written in advance?

A. Because criteria written before you are invested in a deal are honest; criteria written afterwards tend to bend toward what you want to do.

Why this matters

Developers tend to plan meticulously for project risks and barely at all for personal ones. Yet a developer's projects are usually more dependent on him than any employee's job is on them. He signs draw requests, approves changes, negotiates with lenders and holds the relationships. If he dies without a plan, his share of a project may be frozen while a court decides who controls it. If he is incapacitated, nobody may have legal authority to sign. A project that loses its decision-maker for six months can lose its lender, its contractor and its buyers. Protecting the base is not a family matter separate from the business; it is risk management for the business.

Tessa teaches the legal concepts this week; Warrick connects them to the balance sheet. Everything here is conceptual. Laws on wills, powers of attorney and insurance differ by jurisdiction. Verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer licensed where you live and where your assets are, and a licensed insurance adviser.

The four events and their protections

Start from first principles by asking what can happen to the person, not to the project. There are four events.

EventWhat breaksProtection
You dieNobody has clear authority over your assets; the law, not you, decides who inheritsA will, naming an executor
You cannot decideNobody can sign for you on money or health mattersPowers of attorney
A large loss hitsA fire, an injury claim or a lawsuit drains your balance sheetInsurance
Income stopsBills continue while fees and salary pauseAn emergency reserve

A will is a legal document saying who receives your property when you die. It names an executor, the person responsible for gathering your assets, paying your debts and distributing what remains. Without a valid will, most legal systems apply default rules, often called intestacy rules, that decide who inherits according to family relationship. Those rules were written for nobody in particular, and they may not match what you would have chosen.

A power of attorney is a document in which you appoint someone, called your attorney, to act for you. One kind covers money and property; in many places a separate one covers personal and health decisions. The kind that matters most here is designed to continue if you lose mental capacity, because that is exactly when you need it. Whether a power of attorney survives incapacity, and what it must say to do so, depends on the jurisdiction.

Say that out loud now.

"A will speaks when I die. A power of attorney speaks when I cannot."

Insurance and the reserve: transferring and absorbing risk

Insurance is risk transfer: you pay a known, small amount, the premium, so that someone else pays an unknown, large amount if a defined event occurs. The professional framing is to sort risks into those you can absorb from your own reserve and those that could ruin you. Small, frequent losses you generally keep. Large, rare losses you transfer. Life insurance can replace the value your death removes; disability insurance can replace income if illness or injury stops you working; property and liability insurance protect against damage and claims.

The emergency reserve is last week's liquidity floor seen from the protection side. It pays for the losses you have chosen not to insure: the deductible on a claim, a sudden repair, a gap between projects. It also buys time, so that a disability claim's waiting period or an estate's delay does not force a sale.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer aged forty holds a $300,000 share of a project, a home with a $400,000 mortgage, and a personal guarantee on a construction loan. He dies in an accident with no will, no life insurance and $40,000 in savings. Default rules decide who inherits, and a court must appoint someone to administer the estate, which takes time. Meanwhile the lender, whose guarantor has died, may treat the death as a default under the loan. The project needs decisions this month. His share may end up being sold to his partner at a discount simply because nobody had the authority and cash to hold it.

Now the same developer, with protections in place. His will names an executor who understands the business and has authority from day one. A life insurance policy pays a sum that covers the guarantee exposure and the mortgage. His partnership agreement, reviewed alongside the will, says what happens to his share on death. The project continues; his share is either held or sold at a fair price, on a timetable his family chooses.

Incapacity: the forgotten event

People plan for death more readily than for incapacity, yet a period of being unable to decide, through illness, injury or a medical emergency, is a real risk, and its effect on a developer can be worse than death for the business. A will does nothing while you are alive. If you have no valid power of attorney and you cannot act, someone may have to apply to a court for authority to manage your affairs, which can take time and expense, and the person appointed may not be the one you would have picked.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer is hospitalised for three months after a car accident. He is the sole signing officer of his project company and the only person authorised on its bank account. A contractor's progress payment and a loan draw are both due. Without a power of attorney for his personal affairs, and without a second signing authority in the company, nobody can sign. Two controls would have solved it: a power of attorney for property, and a company resolution naming an alternate signatory with defined limits.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming these protections can wait until you are older or richer, then taking on guarantees and project interests with none of them in place. The control is simple and dated: before you sign your next personal guarantee, have a signed will, signed powers of attorney, an insurance review and a funded reserve, each confirmed by the relevant licensed professional.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs a will once, puts it in a drawer and forgets it. Wills, powers of attorney and insurance beneficiaries go stale. Marriages, separations, births, new partners and new projects can all change what the documents should say, and in some jurisdictions certain life events can affect whether a will remains valid. Review the set after every major life event and every major deal.

Callback

Last week, in lesson 43, you learned that net worth hides liquidity and leaves guarantees off the page. This week extends that idea. Your balance sheet also hides who can act on it. A million dollars of assets that nobody has authority to manage is, for a while, worth very little to the people relying on you. Protecting the base means making sure your balance sheet can be operated by someone else.

Recap

Four events can undo a developer regardless of deal quality: death, incapacity, a large loss and lost income. Their protections are a will naming an executor, powers of attorney, insurance, and an emergency reserve. Incapacity is the most neglected. Review all four after every major life event and deal. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer and a licensed insurance adviser.

Next lesson: Ford, with Cole assisting, on the estate of Prince, who died in 2016 without a will.
checklist: Confirm you have a signed, current will naming an executor who can handle business interests.
Confirm you have powers of attorney for property and for personal care that continue through incapacity.
Check that your company has an alternate signing authority with defined limits.
Sort your risks into those your reserve can absorb and those you must insure.
List insurance in force: life, disability, property and liability, with amounts and beneficiaries.
Check that your reserve covers deductibles and waiting periods.
Review the whole set after every major life event and every major deal.
Book an estate lawyer and a licensed insurance adviser before acting.
head: Field checklist
speak: My deals can be excellent and still fail me, because the person running them can die, lose the ability to decide, suffer a large loss or lose income. Each event has a protection. A will names an executor and decides who inherits, instead of default rules written for nobody in particular. Powers of attorney let someone I trust act for me if I cannot, which is the event most people forget, and for a developer it can freeze a project faster than death. Insurance transfers the large, rare losses I could not survive, while my reserve absorbs the small ones and buys time through waiting periods and delays. I also make sure my company has an alternate signing authority. And I review the whole set after every major life event and every major deal. These are concepts: an estate lawyer and a licensed insurance adviser sign off before I act.
terms: Executor — the person named in a will to gather the deceased's assets, pay debts and distribute what remains.
Power of attorney — a document appointing someone to act for you on money, property or personal decisions, which in many places can be made to continue through incapacity.
Risk transfer — paying a known premium so that someone else bears a defined, larger loss if it occurs.

hostile.q: You're our sole guarantor and the only signing officer. What happens to this loan if you're hit by a bus tomorrow?
hostile.a: That is a fair question, and I have an answer on paper. My company has an alternate signing officer with defined limits, appointed by resolution. I have a current will naming an executor who understands the business, and powers of attorney that operate if I am alive but unable to act. Life insurance covers the guarantee exposure, and my partnership agreement says what happens to my share. I can give you a summary of each, and my lawyer can confirm them in writing by Friday.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (audit and integrity)
title: The estate of Prince: a fortune with no instructions
summary: Prince died in April 2016 and no will was ever found. A valuable, complex and hard-to-value estate then spent years in court over who the heirs were, who should manage it and what it was worth. This lesson takes the case through seven forensic steps and ends with Rule 8.
body:
The absence of a will does not mean an absence of rules; it means the rules were written by someone who never met you. Prince's estate shows what that costs when the assets are valuable, complex and hard to value.

Recall

Q. In the personal balance sheet worked example, why were the home and the project share excluded from liquid net worth?

A. Because neither could be turned into cash within about thirty days at anything near fair value.

Q. What are the seven steps of a failure forensics review?

A. Timeline, key decisions, assumptions, incentives, warning signs ignored, point of no return, and root cause, ending with one prevention rule.

Q. What is a decision journal for?

A. To record a decision, your reasons and your expectations at the time, so you can later judge the decision on its quality rather than only on its outcome.

Why this matters

A developer's estate looks a lot like Prince's in one way: much of its value sits in assets that are hard to value, hard to sell quickly and dependent on decisions someone must keep making. A share in a partly built project needs active management just as a music catalogue does. If nobody has clear authority to make those decisions, value leaks away while the authority is being sorted out.

Cole's note on scope: this is an American case decided under one state's law. It teaches how to think, not what the law is where you live. Verify any point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer.

Timeline and key decisions

Step 1, the timeline. Prince Rogers Nelson died on 21 April 2016 at Paisley Park, his home and studio complex in Minnesota. No will was found. Within days, his sister asked the local probate court to appoint someone to take charge of the estate, and the court appointed a bank's trust company as special administrator. Many people came forward claiming to be heirs, and the court had to work through those claims. A different bank later took over as the estate's personal representative. The estate became involved in disputes over management, fees, business deals and its value for tax purposes, including a long-running disagreement with the federal tax authority. Distribution was not completed until roughly six years after his death.

Step 2, the key decisions. The decisive choice is the one that was never made: to sign a will, and with it to choose an executor and set out who should benefit and how the business assets should be run. Other choices followed from that absence. With no named executor, a court had to choose who would manage the assets. With no stated wishes, default inheritance rules decided who the heirs were.

Assumptions and incentives

Step 3, the assumptions. We cannot know what Prince himself assumed, and Ford will not guess at his reasons. What we can name are the assumptions common to people in his position, which the case exposes. That there will be time to do it later. That the people close to you know what you want. That the law will produce a sensible result. That a valuable estate is a simple one. Each fails under pressure. Default rules decide heirs by relationship, not by your wishes, and the value of creative and business assets depends on judgments about how they are managed that the law cannot make for you.

Step 4, the incentives. Cole looks at who was paid and how. When an estate is large and unplanned, many parties acquire a reason to act: claimants who may stand to inherit, advisers and administrators paid from the estate, business partners seeking deals, and a tax authority with an interest in a higher valuation. None of these incentives is improper in itself. Together they create pressure, delay and cost, all paid from the assets the heirs eventually receive.

Warning signs and the point of no return

Step 5, the warning signs ignored. In general terms, for anyone: significant assets, a complex business, relationships and arrangements known only to the owner, and no documented instructions. Each of these alone is common. Together they predict a long and contested administration.

Say that out loud now.

"No will is still a plan. It is just somebody else's plan."

Step 6, the point of no return. The point of no return for an estate plan is the moment the person loses the ability to make one: death or loss of mental capacity. Before it, every option is open and cheap. After it, the options belong to courts and default rules. Notice how ordinary that point is. Nobody knows when it will come.

Root cause and the rule

Step 7, the root cause. The root cause was not a lack of wealth, advisers or access to lawyers. It was the absence of a signed set of instructions for valuable, complex, hard-to-value assets, leaving every key decision about authority, inheritance and management to be settled after the one person who knew the answers could no longer give them.

Now an applied example, hypothetical. A developer holds a 40 percent share in a project company with one partner. He dies without a will. His share passes under default rules to several relatives, none of whom knows the business. Until someone is appointed to act for the estate, nobody can vote his shares. The partner needs a decision on a change order and a loan extension. The shareholder agreement, written years earlier, says nothing clear about death. The lender grows nervous. Within months, the partner offers to buy the share at a steep discount, and the estate, needing cash and certainty, accepts. The value lost was not in the building. It was in the missing instructions.

Cole adds an auditor's point. Even a good will leaves an executor searching if your arrangements live only in your head. Which bank holds the project account? Who is the lender's contact? Where are the shareholder agreement, the guarantee and the insurance policies? What side agreements exist, and with whom? A developer's executor needs a short, dated letter of instructions: not a legal document, but a map to the documents that are. Many estates lose months not to legal disputes but to simply finding things. Keep the letter with your will, update it whenever the document register changes, and tell your executor it exists.

With a will naming an executor who understands development, a shareholder agreement with a clear buy-sell clause triggered by death and priced by a set method, and life insurance to fund it, the same event produces a fair price on a known timetable.

Rule 8: Sign a will and powers of attorney before you sign your first personal guarantee, and review them at every major deal and life event.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing an estate plan is for the old or the very rich. The point of no return can arrive at any age. The control is to treat the will, the powers of attorney and the business agreements as one set, reviewed together before each new guarantee or partnership, with professional sign-off from an estate lawyer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs a will but ignores the business agreements, which often decide what happens to a share in a company regardless of the will. A will can leave your shares to someone; a shareholder agreement may decide whether they can keep them, must sell them, and at what price. Read both together.

Callback

In lesson 44, Olympia and York showed that a point of no return arrives well before the visible failure. The same is true here, and more starkly: the point of no return for an estate plan is the moment you can no longer make one. In both cases, the only good decisions are the early, unhurried ones made while every option is still open.

Recap

Prince died in April 2016 without a will. His estate spent roughly six years on heirship claims, disputes over management and a contest over its value for tax. The root cause was the absence of signed instructions for valuable, complex assets. Rule 8: sign a will and powers of attorney before your first personal guarantee, and review them at every major deal and life event.

Next lesson: Warrick on the money, putting a price on protection and on its absence.
checklist: Confirm you have a signed will and know where the original is kept.
Name an executor who can manage business interests, and an alternate.
Read every shareholder and partnership agreement for what happens on death and incapacity.
Check whether a buy-sell clause has a pricing method and a funding source.
Write down business arrangements that only you currently know about.
Sign powers of attorney before signing any new personal guarantee.
Review the whole set with an estate lawyer at every major deal and life event.
head: Field checklist
speak: Prince died in April 2016 and no will was found. A court appointed an administrator, many people claimed to be heirs, management passed between institutions, and the estate fought a long dispute with the tax authority over its value. Distribution took about six years. The root cause was not a lack of wealth or advisers. It was the absence of signed instructions for valuable, complex, hard-to-value assets, so every decision about authority, inheritance and management was made after the one person who knew the answers could no longer give them. A developer's estate has the same weakness: a project share needs someone with authority to keep deciding. No will is still a plan, just somebody else's. Rule 8: I sign a will and powers of attorney before my first personal guarantee, and I review them, together with my business agreements, at every major deal and life event.
terms: Intestacy — dying without a valid will, so that default legal rules decide who inherits.
Probate — the court process that confirms a will or appoints someone to administer an estate, giving them legal authority to act.
Buy-sell clause — a term in a shareholder or partnership agreement that sets out who must or may buy a departing owner's share, and at what price, on events such as death.

hostile.q: Your partner dies tomorrow. Who controls his half of this project, and how long until we know?
hostile.a: Our shareholder agreement answers that, and I can show you the clause. On a partner's death, the surviving partner has the right to buy the share at a price set by an independent valuation method written into the agreement, and the purchase is funded by insurance each of us holds on the other. Until then, the agreement sets out how the share is voted. Each of us also has a current will naming an executor. I'll have our lawyer confirm the mechanics in writing by Friday.

rule: Rule 8: Sign a will and powers of attorney before you sign your first personal guarantee, and review them at every major deal and life event.

title: The price of protection: premiums, retentions and the cost of delay
summary: Protection costs money every year, and its absence costs money at the worst possible time. This lesson prices insurance as a trade between premiums and retained risk, shows how an unplanned death or incapacity turns into carrying costs and forced-sale discounts on a project, and closes with how large firms structure protection and a Wealth Ledger entry.
body:
Insure what would ruin you, keep what would merely hurt you, and count the cost of delay as a real number. Protection is cheapest when it is bought calmly, sized deliberately and reviewed every year.

Recall

Q. What three questions sit behind a lender's request for a full personal guarantee?

A. How will we get repaid if the project fails? Is the sponsor honest about his finances? Will the sponsor stay and fix problems?

Q. When presenting a number aloud, what three things should travel with it?

A. A rounded figure, what it is compared with, and what it means for the decision.

Q. What is the planning fallacy?

A. The tendency to expect our own plans to go faster, cheaper and more smoothly than similar plans usually do, even when we know the track record of others.

Why this matters

Protection spending is easy to cut because its benefit is invisible in a good year. A developer looking at a premium bill sees money leaving with nothing coming back. To keep protection funded through the years when nothing goes wrong, you need to see both sides in dollars: what you pay every year, and what you would lose in the year something does go wrong.

Premium versus retention

In plain English, every insurance decision is a choice about how much of a loss you keep yourself and how much you pay someone else to take. The part you keep is the retention, which on personal policies usually appears as a deductible or excess, or as a waiting period before benefits start. A higher retention means a lower premium, because the insurer pays less often.

The professional framing: keep the losses your reserve can absorb without strain, and transfer the ones that could breach your liquidity floor. Paying an insurer to handle small, predictable losses is expensive, because the premium includes the insurer's costs and margin on top of the expected losses.

Worked example, hypothetical. A property policy offers two options. With a $1,000 deductible, the premium is $2,400 a year. With a $10,000 deductible, it is $1,800 a year. The higher deductible saves $600 a year and exposes you to an extra $9,000 if you claim. If you would expect a claim roughly once every fifteen years, the extra retained cost averages about $600 a year, close to the saving. The deciding question is therefore not the average but your reserve: can it absorb $10,000 without breaching your floor? If yes, the higher retention is reasonable. If no, the lower one is safer, whatever the arithmetic says.

The cost of delay

The second price is the one rarely written down. When a developer dies or is incapacitated without the right documents, his assets do not vanish. They stop being managed. Every month without authority has a carrying cost: interest on loans, taxes, insurance, maintenance and missed opportunities. And if the delay ends in a rushed sale, a forced-sale discount is added on top.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer's estate holds a 50 percent share in a completed but unsold six-unit project. The project carries a $1,500,000 loan at 8 percent a year, so interest alone is about $10,000 a month. Holding costs such as property tax, insurance and maintenance add another $3,000 a month. The estate's half of those costs is $6,500 a month. If authority takes nine months to establish, the estate bears about $58,500 in carrying costs before a single unit can be sold. If the partner then buys the share at a 20 percent discount to a fair value of $600,000, that is another $120,000 lost. The cost of having no plan: about $178,500. The cost of a will, powers of attorney and a properly funded buy-sell clause is a small fraction of that.

The lender adds a further cost that the example leaves out. Many loan documents treat the death or incapacity of a guarantor as an event the lender may act on, for example by requiring a replacement guarantor or additional security within a set time. Whether and how that applies depends entirely on the wording, which is commercial practice, not a standard. If no replacement can be offered quickly, the estate may face fees, a higher interest rate or pressure to sell. A developer can reduce this cost in advance: read the relevant clauses now, know who could step in as replacement guarantor, and make sure the estate would have cash, from insurance, to offer the lender comfort instead of a fire sale. Delay is expensive in carrying costs alone; delay with an anxious lender is more expensive still.

Say that out loud now.

"Delay has a monthly price, and the estate pays it."

How the best do it

Large construction and development firms generally run protection as a managed programme rather than as a stack of separate policies. A risk manager works with specialist brokers to set retentions according to what the firm's balance sheet can absorb, insures the catastrophic and the uninsurable-without-help, and reviews the whole programme every year against the firm's current projects. Many such firms also plan for the loss of key people, so that the firm's operations continue if a senior leader is suddenly unavailable: deputies with defined authority, documented relationships, and in some cases insurance on key individuals.

What a small developer can copy is the method, not the scale. Write down your retention limit, the largest loss you will absorb from your reserve, and check every policy against it. Insure yourself as a key person in your own business. Review the whole set once a year in the same month, and after each major deal.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, protection appears in three places. Premiums appear as recurring spending, inside the essential monthly figure that sizes your liquidity floor, so cutting them should feel like cutting the floor. Your reserve appears as a liquid asset, with a note that part of it is earmarked to cover retentions. And your insurance cover appears nowhere as an asset, which is correct, but it should appear in a note beside your contingent liabilities, showing which guarantee or debt each policy stands behind. A guarantee with matching life cover is a different risk from one without. Seeing them side by side is how you notice the gap. A licensed adviser is required before you buy or change any policy.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting premiums lapse or cover fall behind your exposure, because the benefit never shows up in a good year. The control is an annual protection review on a fixed date: list every guarantee and debt, list every policy and what it stands behind, confirm retentions fit your reserve, and close any gap with a licensed adviser.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner buys the lowest deductible on everything, pays a high premium to insure small losses he could easily absorb, and then has too little left to insure the large ones. Spend your premium budget on the losses that would ruin you, not on the ones that would only annoy you.

Callback

In lesson 45 you learned that cash drag is the visible cost of a liquidity floor and that averages hide ruin. Insurance works the same way. A premium is a visible, certain cost, and its expected benefit often looks smaller than the premium, because insurers must cover their costs. You buy it anyway for the same reason you hold the floor: it removes the outcome you cannot average away.

Recap

Insurance is a trade between premium and retention: keep the losses your reserve can absorb, transfer the ones that would breach your floor. The absence of a plan has its own price, carrying costs during delay plus a forced-sale discount, which can dwarf the cost of a will and a funded buy-sell clause. Large firms run protection as an annual programme sized to the balance sheet; copy the method.

Next lesson: Tessa on the rules: what makes a will valid, what a power of attorney can do, and why beneficiary designations matter.
checklist: Set a written retention limit: the largest loss you will absorb from your reserve.
Check every deductible and waiting period against that limit.
Calculate the monthly carrying cost of each project you hold an interest in.
Estimate the cost of a nine-month delay plus a forced-sale discount on your largest stake.
Note beside each guarantee and debt which policy, if any, stands behind it.
Include premiums in the essential spending that sizes your liquidity floor.
Hold an annual protection review on a fixed date, with a licensed adviser.
head: Field checklist
speak: Protection has two prices. The first is the premium, which I pay every year whether anything happens or not. Every policy is a trade between premium and retention, the part of a loss I keep. I keep the losses my reserve can absorb and pay to transfer the ones that would breach my floor. The second price is the cost of having no plan. If I die or am incapacitated without the right documents, my share of a project stops being managed but keeps costing money: in my hypothetical, six and a half thousand dollars a month in carrying costs for nine months, then a twenty percent discount when the partner buys the share. That is about a hundred and eighty thousand dollars lost to missing paperwork. Large firms run protection as an annual programme sized to the balance sheet. I copy the method: a retention limit, cover matched to each guarantee, and a yearly review.
terms: Retention — the part of a loss you keep yourself, such as a deductible or waiting period, in exchange for a lower premium.
Carrying cost — the ongoing cost of holding an asset, such as interest, tax, insurance and maintenance, paid whether or not it is earning.
Key-person risk — the risk that a business is damaged by the sudden loss of one individual whose knowledge, relationships or authority it depends on.

hostile.q: You're paying for life and disability cover out of a project budget that's already tight. Isn't that money better spent on the building?
hostile.a: The cover is paid from my personal budget, not the project's, but the question is fair, so here is the comparison. The premiums cost a known amount each year. Without them, my death or disability would leave my share of this project unmanaged and unfunded, with carrying costs of several thousand dollars a month and a likely discounted sale. That outcome hurts the project and every lender and partner in it. The cover is part of what makes me a reliable sponsor.

title: What makes it work: valid wills, enduring powers and beneficiary designations
summary: A will, a power of attorney or an insurance policy protects you only if it is legally effective when needed. This lesson explains, as concepts, what generally makes a will valid, how a power of attorney can survive incapacity, why insurance disclosure matters, and how beneficiary designations can bypass a will altogether.
body:
A protection document that fails a legal test is worse than none, because everyone relied on it. Learn the tests in concept, then let an estate lawyer apply them where you live.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 7?

A. Never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything; size every commitment so its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched.

Q. What can you safely say in writing when you are not sure of a fact?

A. That you will confirm it by a specific date, rather than guessing. A wrong figure in writing can be relied on by others.

Q. Why does caffeine timing matter on a shift schedule?

A. Because caffeine taken too close to your sleep window can disrupt sleep you badly need. Individual responses vary; check that with your doctor.

Why this matters

Many estate disputes are not about what the deceased wanted. They are about whether the document saying what they wanted is legally effective. A will signed without the required formalities, or a power of attorney that does not survive incapacity, can fail at exactly the moment it was written for. Knowing the tests in outline lets you ask your lawyer the right questions and spot the gaps before they matter.

Everything below is conceptual. The tests, the formalities and the consequences differ between jurisdictions and change over time. Verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer licensed in each jurisdiction where you live or hold assets.

What generally makes a will valid

Most legal systems ask a similar set of questions, though the answers differ. Was it made with the formalities the law requires, such as being in writing, signed, and in many places witnessed by people who do not benefit from it? Did the person have testamentary capacity, meaning they understood that they were making a will, broadly what they owned, and who might have a claim on them? Was it their own free choice, rather than the product of undue influence, meaning pressure from someone else that overrode their will? And is it still in force, or has it been revoked by a later will or, in some systems, affected by certain later life events?

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer writes a will by hand on a business trip and signs it, intending to have it witnessed later. He dies before he does. Whether that document counts depends entirely on the jurisdiction: some systems accept a handwritten will without witnesses in defined circumstances, others do not. If it fails, his previous will, or the default rules if there is none, may govern instead. The lesson is not which answer is right. It is that an informal document is a gamble on a rule you have not checked.

Two more rules of thumb to raise with your lawyer. Assets in more than one country can raise questions about which country's law governs which asset, and some people use more than one will for that reason; that is a specialist subject later in the course. And the executor needs the original document, so where it is kept and who knows where it is are practical matters, not afterthoughts.

Executors carry duties, too, and choosing one well means understanding them. In general terms, an executor must gather and protect the assets, find out what the estate owes, pay debts and taxes, keep accounts and only then distribute what remains to the beneficiaries. In many systems an executor who distributes too early, before debts and taxes are settled, can face personal exposure for the shortfall; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. For a developer's estate, that means the executor may need to keep a project share managed and insured for months while valuations, tax filings and partner negotiations run their course. Pick someone with the judgment and the time, name an alternate, and ask them before you name them.

Powers of attorney that survive incapacity

Under traditional rules in many places, an agent's authority ended if the person who granted it lost capacity, which defeated the purpose for the very event people worried about. Many jurisdictions now allow a form of power of attorney designed to continue through incapacity, often called enduring or durable. It usually has to be made while you still have capacity and must meet specific formal requirements.

The professional framing has four questions. Does it continue through incapacity? When does it start: immediately, or only when incapacity is confirmed, and if so, by whom? What can the attorney do: everything, or only defined matters, and can they deal with your business interests? And what controls exist: must they keep accounts, can you name more than one attorney, and must they act together or may each act alone?

Say that out loud now.

"A power of attorney must be made while I can, to work when I cannot."

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer names his business partner as his only attorney for property. He is later incapacitated after an accident. The partner now has authority over the developer's personal assets, including his shares in their joint company, and is on both sides of every decision about that company. That is a conflict of interest built into the document. A better structure might name someone independent of the business, or two attorneys acting jointly, with a duty to keep accounts. The partner's role is better handled in the shareholder agreement.

Insurance contracts and beneficiary designations

Insurance is a contract, and two features matter here. First, insurance law in many places imposes strong duties of disclosure: you must answer the insurer's questions honestly and completely, and in some systems disclose material facts even if not asked. A policy obtained on incomplete answers may be challenged when a claim is made, which is the worst possible time to learn it.

Second, many policies and some accounts let you name a beneficiary directly. In many systems, money paid under a beneficiary designation goes straight to the named person, outside the will and often outside probate. That is powerful and fast, and it is also a common source of error: the designation, not the will, may decide who gets the money. An old designation naming someone who should no longer benefit can override a carefully drafted new will. Check how designations interact with wills where you live.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a document that looks complete but fails a formal test, or a designation that quietly contradicts your will. The control is a document register reviewed with an estate lawyer: every will, power of attorney, policy and designation, its date, where the original is kept, and a note confirming that each one is consistent with the others.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner downloads a template, signs it alone at the kitchen table and considers the matter closed. Templates may not meet local formalities, may not survive incapacity, and rarely deal with business interests. A document that is invalid when needed protects nobody.

Callback

In lesson 46, Omar described the personal financial statement as a representation that a lender relies on. Insurance applications work the same way. Your answers are statements of fact the insurer relies on, and an incomplete answer can undo the policy. Treat every application with the care you would give a statement to a lender: complete, accurate and dated, with your working papers kept.

Recap

A will generally needs the required formalities, testamentary capacity and free choice, and it can be revoked or affected by later events. A power of attorney must be made while you have capacity, in a form designed to continue through incapacity, with clear scope and controls, and free of built-in conflicts. Insurance requires honest disclosure, and beneficiary designations may override your will. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer.

Next lesson: Roman on the numbers, working backward from what your family would need to the cover and reserve that would provide it.
checklist: Confirm your will was signed with the formalities your lawyer says are required.
Know where the original will is kept and make sure your executor knows too.
Confirm each power of attorney continues through incapacity and states when it starts.
Check that no attorney has a built-in conflict with your business interests.
Review every insurance application for complete and accurate answers.
List every beneficiary designation and check it matches your will.
Keep a document register and review it with an estate lawyer.
head: Field checklist
speak: A protection document only protects me if it is legally effective when it is needed. A will generally has to meet formal requirements, like writing, signature and often independent witnesses. I must have testamentary capacity and make it freely, without undue influence, and it can be revoked or affected by later events. A power of attorney has to be made while I have capacity, in a form designed to continue through incapacity, with clear scope, a clear start, and controls, and I avoid naming someone with a built-in conflict, such as my business partner. Insurance is a contract that demands honest disclosure, so an incomplete application can undo the policy when I claim. And beneficiary designations may pay out directly, outside my will, so an old designation can override a new will. These rules differ by jurisdiction, so an estate lawyer signs off on every document.
terms: Testamentary capacity — the mental ability, at the time of making a will, to understand what a will is, broadly what you own, and who might have a claim on you.
Enduring power of attorney — a power of attorney made in a form designed to continue in effect after the person granting it loses mental capacity; also called durable in some places.
Beneficiary designation — a direct nomination, on a policy or account, of who receives the money, which in many systems pays outside the will.

hostile.q: Suppose a sponsor's new will leaves everything to one person, but his life policy still names a former business partner. Which one wins?
hostile.a: In many systems, the designation on the policy decides who receives that money, regardless of the will, so nobody should assume the will controls it. That is exactly why I keep my own document register and check designations against the will every year. If I found a mismatch like that in my own papers, I would correct the designation with the insurer immediately, confirm in writing that the change was accepted, and ask my estate lawyer to verify how the two interact where I live.

title: Working backward: from what the household needs to the cover and reserve required
summary: A reverse-engineered calculation. Start from the finished outcome you want if a hypothetical developer dies or becomes disabled, then work backward step by step to the life cover, the reserve and the gap. All numbers are hypothetical, and a licensed adviser is required before acting.
body:
Do not start by asking how much insurance to buy. Start by writing down what must be true for the people who rely on you the day after the worst happens, then work backward to the cover and the cash that would make it true.

Recall

Q. What are the four events that can undo a developer regardless of deal quality?

A. Death, incapacity, a large loss, and lost income. Their protections are a will, powers of attorney, insurance and an emergency reserve.

Q. In a numbers lesson, why round figures before saying them aloud?

A. Because listeners cannot hold exact figures in their heads; a rounded number with a clear comparison carries the meaning without the noise.

Q. What is a contingent liability?

A. An obligation that becomes yours only if something else happens, such as a lender calling a personal guarantee.

Why this matters

Most people buy insurance forward: a salesperson suggests an amount, it sounds large, they sign. Reverse engineering puts you in control. You define the outcome, and the arithmetic tells you the cover. This is the method Roman uses on the lender's side too: start from the repayment you need, and work back to what must be in place to produce it. This week is an even-numbered week, so the whole lesson runs backward.

Every figure is hypothetical and rounded. To keep the arithmetic visible, future income is not discounted for the time value of money; Week 11 teaches that adjustment, and an adviser's figure will include it. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Example 1, death: start from the finished outcome

Step 1. Write the outcome. If the developer dies tomorrow, the people who depend on him should be able to: own their home outright; have the personal guarantee on his project covered so the lender cannot reach the household; replace the after-tax income he provided for ten years; pay the final costs of the estate; and keep their own emergency reserve.

Step 2. Put a number on each item. Mortgage payoff: $400,000. Guarantee exposure, at its cap: $250,000. Income replacement: $60,000 a year for ten years, $600,000. Estate and final costs: $30,000. Household emergency reserve: $40,000.

Step 3. Add them up. $400,000 plus $250,000 plus $600,000 plus $30,000 plus $40,000 equals $1,320,000. That is the total need.

Step 4. Subtract what already exists and would be available quickly. Liquid assets: $88,000. Existing group life cover through an employer or association: $100,000. Total available: $188,000. Note what is excluded: the project share. It may be worth $300,000, but it cannot be relied on to become cash quickly at fair value, and it may be subject to a buy-sell clause.

Step 5. Calculate the gap. $1,320,000 minus $188,000 equals $1,132,000. That is the additional life cover the outcome requires, before an adviser refines it.

Step 6. Test the pieces for duration. Not every need lasts equally long. The guarantee falls away when the building is completed and leased, perhaps in three years. The mortgage declines as it is paid. Income replacement matters for as long as people depend on that income. This is why a developer's cover is often built in layers with different terms, rather than one policy sized for the peak. Which structure fits is a decision for a licensed adviser.

Say that out loud now.

"Need one point three two million. Have one eighty-eight thousand. Gap one point one three million."

Step 7. Test the sensitivity. A needs analysis is only as good as its assumptions, so change the one you are least sure of and watch the gap move. If income must be replaced for fifteen years instead of ten, income replacement rises from $600,000 to $900,000, the total need from $1,320,000 to $1,620,000, and the gap from $1,132,000 to $1,432,000. One assumption moved the answer by $300,000. If the guarantee cap were negotiated down from $250,000 to $150,000, the gap would fall by $100,000. That second sensitivity matters: sometimes the cheapest way to close a protection gap is not to buy more insurance, but to give a smaller guarantee. Write down which assumptions drive the answer, and revisit them at every review.

Example 2, disability: working back to the reserve

Disability is more likely than death during a working life, and it is harder on a household's cash, because the person is alive and still has costs. Disability insurance often pays only after a waiting period, sometimes called an elimination period, which can be months long. During that period, the reserve carries everything.

Step 1. Write the outcome. If the developer becomes unable to work, the household can pay every essential bill, without selling anything, until disability benefits begin, and can absorb one unexpected large cost during that time.

Step 2. Put numbers on it. Essential monthly spending: $6,000. Waiting period on the hypothetical policy: 90 days, or three months. Add a one-month buffer, because a first payment is often processed after the waiting period ends: four months in total. Unexpected cost to absorb: the $10,000 property deductible from last lesson's example.

Step 3. Calculate the reserve needed. Four months times $6,000 is $24,000, plus $10,000, equals $34,000.

Step 4. Compare with what exists. Liquid assets are $88,000, but the liquidity floor already claims $72,000 of them for twelve months of spending. Is the disability reserve additional, or part of the floor? Logically it is part of it: the floor exists for exactly this kind of shock. The check is that the floor is at least as large as the disability reserve, and here $72,000 comfortably exceeds $34,000.

Step 5. Now reverse the question. What waiting period could this household afford? The floor of $72,000, less the $10,000 deductible, leaves $62,000. Divided by $6,000 a month, that is a little over ten months. A longer waiting period lowers the premium. A household with a strong floor may be able to choose a longer one, and a household without a floor cannot. Your reserve and your insurance are designed together.

Reading the result

The professional framing is to present the result as three lines a lender or adviser can check: the outcome you defined, the total it requires, and the gap after what exists. Then state the duration of each need. Showing your working this way also protects you from the opposite error: buying cover far beyond what any defined outcome requires, which drains cash that the floor needed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is counting illiquid assets, such as a project share or a home, as if they would be available to the household on the day they are needed. The control is to exclude anything that cannot become cash within about thirty days at near fair value, and to treat a project share as worth nothing in the calculation until a funded buy-sell clause says otherwise.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sizes cover forward, from a round number that feels large, and forgets the guarantee. Then the lender's claim on the estate eats the insurance proceeds that were meant for the household. Every guarantee belongs in Step 2.

Callback

In lesson 47, Nadia built the liquidity floor from real monthly spending. Today that same floor did a second job: it set the longest disability waiting period the household could afford. One well-built number serving two decisions is a sign the balance sheet is working as a system, not as a list.

Recap

Work backward. Write the outcome, price each part, add them, subtract only what is quickly available, and the remainder is the gap. Test each need for its duration, because guarantees burn off and mortgages decline. For disability, the waiting period is paid from your reserve, so the reserve and the policy are designed together. A licensed adviser refines and signs off on the numbers.

Next lesson: Tessa in the room, at your first meeting with an estate lawyer.
checklist: Write the outcome you want for the household before looking at any policy.
Price each element: mortgage, guarantees at their caps, income replacement, final costs, reserve.
Subtract only assets that become cash within about thirty days at near fair value.
Treat a project share as zero in the calculation unless a funded buy-sell clause applies.
Note how long each need lasts, especially guarantees that burn off.
Check that your floor covers the disability waiting period plus one large retention.
Take the gap and the durations to a licensed adviser for refinement.
head: Field checklist
speak: I size protection backward. First I write the outcome: if I die tomorrow, the household owns the home outright, the guarantee is covered so the lender cannot reach them, ten years of income is replaced, final costs are paid, and a reserve remains. In my hypothetical, that adds up to one point three two million dollars. Then I subtract only what is quickly available, eighty-eight thousand in liquid assets and a hundred thousand of existing cover, and I exclude the project share because it may not become cash. The gap is about one point one three million. Then I check duration, because the guarantee burns off at completion and the mortgage declines, so cover is often layered. For disability, the waiting period is paid from my reserve: four months of six thousand plus a ten-thousand-dollar deductible is thirty-four thousand, well inside my floor. A licensed adviser signs off.
terms: Needs analysis — sizing protection by first defining the outcome you want and pricing what it requires, rather than starting from a policy amount.
Coverage gap — the difference between what a defined outcome requires and the cover and quickly available assets that already exist.
Waiting period — the time after a disability begins before benefits start, also called an elimination period, during which your reserve carries the costs.

hostile.q: Your proposal shows over a million dollars of life cover. Isn't that just an insurance salesman's number?
hostile.a: No, it is my number, and I can show you how I built it. I started from an outcome: the home owned outright, the project guarantee covered, ten years of income replaced, final costs paid and a reserve left. I priced each item, added them, subtracted only assets that would be available as cash quickly, and the gap is the figure you see. I also split it by duration, because the guarantee portion falls away at completion. A licensed adviser will refine it, but every line can be checked.

title: The first meeting with an estate lawyer
summary: A realistic scene: a developer's first meeting with an estate lawyer. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the questions behind the lawyer's questions, when to stay silent while you think, and how to keep the meeting focused on decisions rather than paperwork.
body:
An estate lawyer can only protect what you disclose and draft what you decide. Arrive with your documents organised and your decisions thought through, and the meeting becomes an hour of judgment instead of an hour of fact-finding.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the estate of Prince?

A. The absence of signed instructions for valuable, complex, hard-to-value assets, leaving decisions about authority, inheritance and management to courts and default rules.

Q. What is the acknowledge, bridge, answer pattern?

A. Acknowledge the concern behind a hostile question, bridge to the relevant fact, then answer it directly or commit to a dated follow-up.

Q. What is inversion as a thinking tool?

A. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid those things.

Why this matters

Most people meet an estate lawyer once every several years. A developer's affairs change faster than that: new companies, new partners, new guarantees. Your first meeting sets the structure everything later is built on, and good lawyers charge for their time. Preparation saves money, and more importantly it makes sure the documents fit your real situation, including the business interests that most templates ignore.

This is a composite scene. The law it touches differs between jurisdictions; verify any point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer licensed where you live and where your assets are.

The scene

You are in a lawyer's office. On the table is your folder: a personal balance sheet, a guarantee schedule, every shareholder and partnership agreement, your insurance policies with their beneficiary designations, and a one-page note of what you want to happen. The lawyer reads for a few minutes, then asks: "Who depends on you financially? Do you own anything outside this country? And has anyone suggested what should go into your will?"

The questions behind the questions

Each of those questions is doing a specific job. "Who depends on you?" helps the lawyer understand who might have a legal claim on your estate whatever the will says; in some systems certain dependants can ask a court to vary a will that leaves them without support. "Anything outside this country?" asks whether more than one legal system will touch your estate, which can affect how documents are drafted and whether more than one will is advisable. "Has anyone suggested what should go in?" is a quiet check for undue influence; the lawyer must be satisfied the instructions are yours. Answer plainly. A lawyer who asks the third question is protecting the will from later challenge, not accusing you.

Lines to say.

  • "Here is everything I own and everything I have guaranteed, with values and dates."
  • "For each company, what happens to my share if I die, and what happens if I am alive but cannot act?"
  • "Do my shareholder agreements and my will say the same thing? If not, which one controls?"
  • "Who would you suggest as executor and attorney, given that my assets need business judgment?"
  • "What is your fee for this work, what does it include, and what would cost extra?"

Lines never to say.

  • "Just use your standard will." Standard documents rarely handle business interests well.
  • "My partner and I have an understanding about that." An understanding that is not written will not bind an executor or a court.
  • "Can we leave that company out of the paperwork?" Omitting assets from your lawyer leaves them unplanned, and concealment can create far worse problems.
  • "I'll sort out the insurance designations later." Designations may bypass the will entirely; they belong in this meeting.
  • "Make my partner my attorney for everything." That builds a conflict of interest into the document.

Say that out loud now.

"For each company: what happens to my share if I die, and what happens if I cannot act?"

Silence, decisions and state

At some point the lawyer will ask a question you have not decided: who should receive what, who should be trusted with authority, what should happen to a business if nobody in the family wants to run it. Do not answer to fill the silence. Say: "I need to think about that properly. Can I come back to you by Friday with a written answer?" A considered answer in writing is worth more than a quick one in the room, and it is better evidence of your own free choice.

Notice the difference between facts and decisions. Facts are what you own and owe; bring them complete. Decisions are who gets what and who decides; bring your thinking, but let the lawyer explain the options before you commit.

Worked example, hypothetical. You hold 50 percent of a project company. Your shareholder agreement gives the surviving partner a right to buy your share on death at a price set by an annual valuation, but neither of you has updated the valuation in three years. The lawyer flags it: the clause works only if the price is current and the purchase is funded. Your action list leaves the room with three items: update the valuation, check that each partner holds insurance to fund the purchase, and make sure your will points your executor toward the clause rather than fighting it.

Second worked example, hypothetical. The lawyer asks who should hold your power of attorney. Your first instinct is your business partner. The lawyer points out the conflict. Together you design it differently: a trusted person independent of the business as your attorney for personal property, a company resolution naming your partner as alternate signing officer for company matters only, with defined limits, and a duty on your attorney to keep accounts.

As for state, these meetings can be heavy; nobody enjoys planning for their own death or incapacity. Treat it as a design session for a system, which is what it is. If you notice yourself rushing to finish, slow down. The quality of these documents will matter more than almost anything else you sign this year.

After the meeting

The meeting is not the finish line. Read the draft documents slowly, out loud if it helps, and check every name, share and condition against your one-page note. Sign them the way the lawyer tells you to, with the required witnesses present, rather than at home alone. Agree where the originals will be kept and tell your executor and attorney where that is. Then update your document register and your letter of instructions the same day. A plan that exists only in the lawyer's file, unknown to the people who must use it, is barely better than no plan.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is incomplete disclosure: a company, a guarantee, an overseas asset or an old beneficiary designation that never reaches the lawyer and therefore never reaches the plan. The control is the folder: a complete balance sheet, guarantee schedule, every business agreement and every policy, checked against your own records before the meeting.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner arrives with nothing, spends the paid hour listing assets from memory, decides everything on the spot, and never mentions the shareholder agreements. Facts should arrive on paper; decisions should be made after the options are explained.

Callback

In lesson 48, Roman taught you to answer a lender's real questions with evidence and to stay silent after making a proposal. The estate lawyer's meeting uses the same skills from the other side of the table. You bring the evidence in a folder, you recognise the purpose behind each question, and you use silence not to pressure anyone but to give yourself time to decide well.

Recap

Arrive with a complete folder: balance sheet, guarantees, business agreements, policies and designations. Understand what the lawyer's questions are for: possible claims, foreign assets, and confirming the instructions are yours. Say what each company needs on death and on incapacity. Never ask for a standard will, rely on unwritten understandings, or hide an asset. Take time over decisions. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer.

Next lesson: Kema with the week's six questions and Cole's Auditor's Chair.
checklist: Bring a complete folder: balance sheet, guarantee schedule, business agreements, policies and designations.
Write a one-page note of what you want to happen before the meeting.
Ask, for each company, what happens on your death and on your incapacity.
Ask whether your shareholder agreements and will are consistent, and which controls.
Avoid naming a business partner as attorney for everything.
Ask for the fee, what it covers and what costs extra.
Defer undecided questions to a dated written answer.
Leave with an action list and a date to sign.
head: Field checklist
speak: At my first meeting with an estate lawyer, I bring facts on paper and leave time for decisions. The folder holds my balance sheet, my guarantee schedule, every shareholder and partnership agreement, my insurance policies and their beneficiary designations, and a one-page note of what I want. I understand why the lawyer asks who depends on me, whether I own anything abroad, and whether anyone suggested what should go in: possible claims, more than one legal system, and confirming the instructions are mine. For each company I ask what happens to my share if I die and if I cannot act, and whether my agreements and my will agree. I never ask for a standard will, rely on an unwritten understanding with a partner, or leave an asset out. When a decision is hard, I say I will answer in writing by Friday.
terms: Dependant's claim — in some legal systems, a right of a person who relied on the deceased for support to ask a court to vary a will that leaves them without adequate provision.
Undue influence — pressure from another person that overrides a will-maker's free choice, which can make a will open to challenge.
Alternate signing officer — a person authorised by company resolution to sign for the company, within defined limits, if the usual signatory cannot.

hostile.q: Your shareholder agreement says your partner can buy your share on death at the last annual valuation. When was the last valuation, and how would he pay for it?
hostile.a: I checked before this meeting. The valuation is out of date, which means the clause would currently produce a price that does not reflect the project. I have an action to update it and to agree with my partner that it is refreshed every year. On funding, each of us is arranging insurance on the other's life sized to the updated value, so the purchase would not depend on either of us raising cash in a hurry. I'll confirm both items in writing by Friday.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 8 review: protecting the base, and Cole's Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions with answers on wills, powers of attorney, insurance, reserves and the Prince case. Then Cole's Auditor's Chair: a hypothetical protection summary read the way a hostile auditor would read it. Finally a two-minute boardroom drill with a model answer.
body:
This week you learned that a developer's wealth needs four protections and that each one works only if it is legally effective, properly sized and kept current. Today you test it, then read a protection plan the way a hostile auditor would.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between premium and retention?

A. The premium is what you pay an insurer each period. The retention is the part of a loss you keep, such as a deductible or waiting period. A higher retention lowers the premium.

Q. What should a strong close to a two-minute explanation contain?

A. The decision or the ask, stated plainly, so the listener knows what you want from them.

Q. What does "bottom line first" protect you from in a meeting?

A. Losing the listener before you reach the point. If you are interrupted after one sentence, they already have your conclusion.

Why this matters

Protection plans fail quietly. Nobody tests a will or a power of attorney until the day it is needed, and by then any flaw is permanent. The only rehearsal available is the one you run now: recall the principles, then attack your own documents as an auditor would.

The six questions

Question 1. Which of the four events is most often left unplanned, and why does it hit a developer hard?

Answer: Incapacity. A will does nothing while you are alive, so without a power of attorney and an alternate signing officer, nobody may have authority to sign draws, payments or loan documents while you cannot act.

Question 2. What is Rule 8, and which case produced it?

Answer: Sign a will and powers of attorney before you sign your first personal guarantee, and review them at every major deal and life event. It came from the estate of Prince, who died in 2016 without a will; the estate took roughly six years to resolve.

Question 3. How do you decide what to insure and what to keep?

Answer: Keep losses your reserve can absorb without breaching your liquidity floor; transfer losses that would breach it. Paying an insurer to carry small, predictable losses is expensive.

Question 4. Why might a beneficiary designation matter more than your will?

Answer: In many systems, money paid under a designation goes directly to the named person, outside the will. An out-of-date designation can override a carefully drafted new will. Verify how this works where you live.

Question 5. In a reverse-engineered needs analysis, why is the project share excluded?

Answer: Because it may not become cash quickly at fair value, and a buy-sell clause may control its sale. Counting it would overstate what the household could rely on.

Question 6. Why should a business partner not be your only attorney for property?

Answer: Because they would be on both sides of every decision about your shared company, a conflict of interest built into the document. Handle company authority through a resolution with defined limits instead.

Say that out loud now.

Say Rule 8 from memory, then name the four events and their four protections without looking.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Once a month, Cole replaces the Red Pen with a harder exercise. You read a document not as its author but as a hostile auditor whose job is to find what would fail under pressure. Here is a short hypothetical protection summary prepared by a developer.

"Protection summary. Will: signed nine years ago, original at home somewhere; it names my brother as executor. Power of attorney: my business partner holds a general power covering everything. Life cover: $500,000, beneficiary is my estate, policy applied for in a hurry before a loan closing. Guarantees: one $1,000,000 guarantee on our current project, joint and several with my partner. Reserve: covered by the $80,000 contingency in the project account. Shareholder agreement: says nothing about death; we agreed verbally we would sort it out."

Cole reads it and asks the questions an auditor would.

  1. "The will is nine years old and predates the current project and guarantee. What has changed since, and has anyone checked whether it still reflects your affairs and remains valid where you live?"
  2. "Where exactly is the original? 'At home somewhere' means your executor may not find it."
  3. "Your partner holds a general power covering everything, including your shares in your joint company. Who protects your interest when he votes your shares on his own deal?"
  4. "Life cover of $500,000 against a $1,000,000 joint and several guarantee: if the lender calls it, what is left for anyone else? And paid to the estate, does the money go through probate and become reachable by the estate's creditors?"
  5. "The application was rushed before a closing. Were all the insurer's questions answered completely? An incomplete answer could put the claim at risk."
  6. "The project contingency belongs to the project. Counting it as your personal reserve means you have no personal reserve."
  7. "A verbal agreement about death is not an agreement an executor can enforce. What happens to your share on day one?"

Every one of those questions is answerable, and every one is cheaper to answer now than after the event.

Here is what good answers look like for three of them. On the power of attorney: "My attorney for personal property is a trusted person outside the business, with a duty to keep accounts; my partner is an alternate signing officer for the company only, within limits set by resolution." On the cover: "Cover has been sized backward from a defined outcome, including the guarantee at its full amount, and each policy names the right beneficiary, checked against my will." On the reserve: "My personal reserve is held in my own account and sized from my essential spending; the project contingency stays with the project and is never counted twice." Notice that every good answer names a document, a person and a number. An answer that relies on intention, trust or memory is the answer an auditor marks down.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes, aloud and timed, before reading the model.

Model answer: "My bottom line: our projects depend on me personally, so protecting myself is risk management for the business. Four events can undo us regardless of deal quality: my death, my incapacity, a large uninsured loss, and a stop in my income. The protections are a current will with an executor who understands the business, powers of attorney that continue through incapacity, insurance sized backward from a defined outcome, and a reserve that covers retentions and waiting periods. The estate of Prince, who died in 2016 without a will, showed what happens otherwise: years of disputes over heirs, management and value. Our controls are an alternate signing officer, a buy-sell clause with a current valuation and insurance to fund it, and an annual review. The ask: approve funding for the cross-insurance and a yearly valuation update."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that this week's lessons feel complete because you understood them, while the documents themselves remain unsigned or out of date. The control is a dated action: book the estate lawyer and the insurance adviser before you finish this week.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner audits other people's documents brilliantly and never his own. Run Cole's questions on your own folder, honestly, and write down every one you cannot answer today.

Callback

In lesson 49, the Red Pen drill caught a developer counting a project contingency as personal liquidity. The same defect appeared in today's protection summary. Repeated errors are not a coincidence; they are what people do when the project's money and their own are not clearly separated. Separate accounts and separate records make that error impossible.

Recap

Four events, four protections: will, powers of attorney, insurance and reserve. Each must be legally effective, sized backward from a defined outcome, consistent with the business agreements, and reviewed at every major deal and life event. The auditor's habit is to ask what fails under pressure, before the pressure arrives.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about protecting the base. My projects depend on me, so four events can undo them regardless of deal quality: my death, my incapacity, a large uninsured loss, and a stop in my income. The protections are a current will with an executor who understands business, powers of attorney that continue through incapacity, insurance sized backward from a defined outcome, and a reserve that covers retentions and waiting periods. Each must be legally effective, consistent with my shareholder agreements, and reviewed at every major deal. The estate of Prince, who died in 2016 without a will, took about six years to resolve. Rule 8: I sign a will and powers of attorney before my first personal guarantee. And I audit my own folder the way a hostile auditor would: old will, conflicted attorney, cover smaller than the guarantee, contingency counted as reserve, a verbal buy-sell. Each is cheaper to fix now.
terms: Auditor's Chair — reading a document as a hostile auditor would, asking what would fail under pressure rather than what the author intended.
Document register — a list of every protection document and designation, with its date, location of the original, and a note on consistency with the others.
Cross-insurance — an arrangement where business partners insure each other's lives so a buy-sell purchase can be funded on death.

hostile.q: You say you've protected the base. When did you last read your own will, and does it match your current companies?
hostile.a: I read it this week as part of the review. It predates my current project and the guarantee I have given, so I have flagged it for updating rather than assume it still fits. I have a document register listing my will, powers of attorney, policies and designations, with the date of each and where the originals are kept, and I have a meeting booked with my estate lawyer to bring everything into line with my business agreements. I'll confirm the signing date to you once it is set.
